front: Nonoverlapping 2.4 GHz channels in the usual North American 20 MHz plan?
back: 1, 6 and 11. This is a reuse plan; the actual permitted channel list depends on the regulatory domain.

front: Why do neighboring 2.4 GHz channel numbers overlap?
back: Centers are generally 5 MHz apart while the occupied channel is much wider, commonly 20 MHz (legacy DSSS about 22 MHz).

front: What happens when 5 GHz 20 MHz channels are bonded to 80 MHz?
back: It consumes the component channels, overlaps their spectrum and leaves fewer independent choices. A higher possible PHY rate is not guaranteed better application throughput.

front: What is DFS for?
back: Protecting radar users on designated shared channels. Detection can force a channel change; exact channels and timing are location/platform dependent.

front: What must support a 6 GHz WLAN?
back: The AP and client need suitable radio capability and local authorization; use the applicable WPA3 or Enhanced Open security design.

front: What does a +3 dB power change mean approximately?
back: Twice the power. It does not mean twice the coverage distance or twice the application throughput.

front: dB versus dBm versus dBi?
back: dB is a ratio; dBm is power relative to 1 mW; dBi is antenna gain relative to an isotropic reference.

front: How is SNR calculated from dBm readings?
back: Signal minus noise at the same receiver and observation period, expressed in dB. −65 − (−92) = 27 dB.

front: What does Wi-Fi 6E add to compatible Wi-Fi 6 equipment?
back: Operation in the 6 GHz band, subject to AP/client support and local authorization. A label or SSID setting does not add a radio band.

front: SSID versus BSSID?
back: SSID is the WLAN name, up to 32 octets. BSSID is a 48-bit service-set identifier, not proof of a particular physical AP.

front: How do an infrastructure BSS and an ESS differ?
back: A BSS is one AP service and its associated stations. An ESS connects infrastructure BSSs through a distribution system.

front: Co-channel versus adjacent-channel effects?
back: Co-channel cells share airtime; overlapping occupied channels can interfere. Either situation can involve retries; there is no fixed throughput-halving rule.

front: What evidence identifies a non-Wi-Fi interferer?
back: Correlate band, time, spectrum information and a controlled change. A nearby microwave or Bluetooth device is a candidate, not proof by itself.

front: Which protection pair does the WPA2-Personal lab use?
back: A shared passphrase with AES-CCMP. WEP and original WPA/TKIP are legacy alternatives, not equivalent modern settings.

front: What changes with WPA3-Personal?
back: SAE password authentication and required PMF. These do not prevent all disruption, protect every management frame or secure a compromised endpoint.

front: Shared Personal credentials versus Enterprise credentials?
back: Ordinary shared-passphrase Personal access differs from individually managed 802.1X/EAP Enterprise authentication. Session enforcement remains a separate policy issue.

front: Omnidirectional and directional antenna patterns?
back: Omni provides coverage around an axis; patch, Yagi and dish designs focus energy in chosen directions. Use actual beamwidth/gain specifications, not a universal ranking.

front: Does strong received signal prove usable application connectivity?
back: No. Check airtime/noise, security, IP settings and the actual service; signal strength establishes only part of the link.

front: Why might increasing AP power fail to repair client uploads?
back: It improves what the client hears, not what the AP hears from the client. Assess both directions and the actual application.

front: Do different SSIDs create separate airtime on the same channel?
back: No. Nearby transmissions still share or interfere with the occupied spectrum; a network name is not a separate radio channel.
